# A lakehouse table inside Postgres

[pg_ducklake](https://github.com/relytcloud/pg_ducklake) adds a column-oriented table to Postgres.
`CREATE TABLE ... USING ducklake` writes the rows as Parquet files in the
[DuckLake](https://ducklake.select) format, keeps the table's catalog (its files, statistics and
snapshots) in ordinary tables in the `ducklake` schema of the same database, and runs every query
that touches the table in DuckDB, which the extension embeds in the Postgres backend. One database
can then hold row tables for the application and column tables for analytics, and a single query can
join the two. Run this statement to make a columnar copy of a table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE events_lake USING ducklake AS SELECT * FROM events;
```

## Scans and lookups

The [pg_ducklake notebook](../notebooks/pg_ducklake_playground.ipynb) builds the same table of five
million events twice, as an ordinary heap with a primary key and as a copy made with
`USING ducklake`:

| | heap | DuckLake |
|---|---|---|
| on disk | 301 MB, plus a 107 MB primary key | 78 MB, one Parquet file |
| sum of amount by device | 159 ms | 33 ms |
| daily distinct users | 1,618 ms | 774 ms |
| top ten users by spend | 453 ms | 52 ms |
| one row by id | 0.12 ms | 13 ms |

The three analytical queries read a few columns of every row, which is the access pattern for Parquet.
DuckDB reads only those columns in vectors of 2,048 values, and answered
2 to 9 times faster than the heap, even though Postgres scanned the heap with two parallel workers.

Fetching a single row works the other way round. A lake table has no index, so DuckDB skips the files
and row groups whose min/max statistics rule the row out and scans the rest, while the heap only
descends a B-tree. Rows that the application reads one at a time therefore belong in heap tables.

## Writes on immutable files

Parquet files are never changed in place, so DuckLake handles small writes separately. An insert
below a row limit is **inlined** into a Postgres table in the catalog, where queries read it
alongside the Parquet until a flush, or the extension's background worker, writes it out. An update
or delete writes a **delete file** that lists the row positions that no longer count. In the
notebook, updating 1,000 rows and deleting 1,663 left the 78 MB data file untouched and added a
14 kB delete file and a 19 kB file with the updated rows.

## Snapshots, time travel and a change feed

Every commit is a snapshot in the catalog, with a record of what it changed. `time_travel` reads the
table as it was at any snapshot that has not been expired, and `table_changes` returns the rows
inserted, updated and deleted between two snapshots, which is what an incremental job downstream
needs:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM ducklake.time_travel('events_lake'::regclass, 5) t;
SELECT * FROM ducklake.table_changes('events_lake'::regclass, 8, 9);
```

After the update and delete the table had 4,998,337 rows, while its snapshot from before them still
had 5,000,001.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A rough edge in 1.0.2

`table_changes` over a range that contains a delete fails with `function struct_pack(...) does not
exist`. Afterwards, that connection's DuckDB has lost its catalog until it reconnects, and even
`DROP TABLE` fails. Ranges of inserts work, so the notebook stays on those.
:::

## Partitions

`CALL ducklake.set_partition('events_part'::regclass, 'device')` makes later writes split their
files by device, so that a filter on device can skip whole files. On a local disk at this size it
made no difference (28 ms for the partitioned table against 30 ms for the single file), because
reading one compressed column of a 78 MB file is already cheap and the row-group statistics inside
the file do part of a partition's job. Partitions matter more on object storage, where a skipped file
is a skipped download, and `ducklake.default_table_path` points the files at S3, GCS, R2 or Azure.

## Joining rows and columns

A lake table can be joined with any Postgres table in plain SQL. DuckDB plans the whole statement and
reads the heap side through its own Postgres scan, as the condensed plan shows:

```text
HASH_JOIN  user_id = user_id
├── DUCKLAKE_SCAN            Table: events_lake   Projections: user_id
└── PGDUCKDB_POSTGRES_SCAN   Table: users         Projections: user_id, pro
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## DuckLake or Doris

pg_ducklake keeps one database and one transaction boundary, and its analytical tables are written by
the same SQL. [Doris](doris.qmd) is a second system to run, but
it scales out on its own hardware and keeps analytical load off the primary. A Postgres server that
runs DuckDB queries is still one server, so heavy analytics there compete with the application for
CPU and memory.
:::
